1

Reading · how friendships change

1.1 Discuss. Is there someone you used to speak to every day and now never speak to? What happened?

KEY WORDS

a network the people you know well

repetition doing the same thing again and again

the exception the unusual case, not the rule

bleak depressing, without much hope

We Used to Talk Every Day

When I was fifteen, I used to phone my best friend every evening at seven o'clock. We never had anything new to say — we had been at school together all day — but we would talk for an hour anyway. My mother used to stand in the hallway making increasingly impatient gestures at the clock. I have not spoken to that friend for nine years.

Nothing happened. That is the part people find hardest to believe. We didn't fall out; nobody said anything cruel; there was no dramatic final conversation. She moved to another city for university, I stayed where I was, and the calls simply got shorter. Then they became messages. Then they became birthdays. There was never a single moment when either of us decided to stop.

Researchers who study friendship say this is the normal pattern rather than the exception. Most adults replace roughly half of their close network every seven years, and usually don't notice it happening. Friendships, unlike families, have no structure holding them up: nobody organises a dinner because it is your friendship's anniversary, and no one expects you at their table on a Sunday. What keeps a friendship alive, it turns out, is mostly repetition — being in the same place, at the same time, often.

That sounds bleak, but I have come to think it is useful. If friendships survive on repetition rather than on the strength of anybody's feelings, then they can be repaired by repetition too. I used to believe that people who genuinely cared would stay in touch automatically, and that silence therefore meant something. I don't believe that any more. Last month I sent that friend a photograph of the two of us at fifteen. She replied in four minutes.

Grammar · used to, would and usually

PRESENTATION

used to + infinitive — a past habit or state that is no longer true:

I used to phone her every evening. · I didn't use to like coffee.

would + infinitive — a repeated past action (not a state); common in stories:

Every evening we would talk for an hour. NOT I would have long hair.

usually / normally + present simple — a habit that is true now:

I usually text her rather than call.

Then — used to / would

Now — usually / normally

I used to call her every evening.

I usually send a message.

We would meet straight after school.

We normally meet once a month.

She didn't use to like big cities.

She usually stays in Tashkent now.

Did you use to live here?

Do you usually work at home?

ERROR WARNING

After did, use use to — no -d:

Did you used to live here? ✗ Did you use to live here? ✓

I didn't used to smoke. ✗ I didn't use to smoke. ✓

would cannot describe a past state:

I would have long hair. ✗ I used to have long hair. ✓

REMEMBER

Two structures that look the same but are completely different:

used to + infinitive = a past habit that has stopped: I used to get up at six. (I don't now.)

be used to + -ing / noun = accustomed to something: I'm used to getting up at six. (It's normal for me now.)

Vocabulary · multi-word verbs

A multi-word verb = verb + particle, with a brand-new meaning:

bring up a child take after a parent look after someone grow up

split up get together catch up with someone put up with something

Inseparable: take after her NOT take her after

VOCABULARY NOTE

With separable verbs, a pronoun goes in the middle:

She brought him up. NOT She brought up him.

Some verbs are inseparable — nothing can come between the parts:

He takes after his father. NOT He takes his father after.

put up with has two particles and is never separated: I can't put up with it.

Everyday English · showing interest and asking for more

4.1 Read the conversation.

Zarina My cousin's moving back to Tashkent next month.

Bek Is she? That's great news.

Zarina Yes — she's been in Almaty for six years.

Bek Six years! So what made her come back?

Zarina Her mother isn't well, and she wants to look after her.

Bek Oh, I'm sorry to hear that. How's she coping?

Zarina Better than I expected, actually.

Showing interest

Asking for more

Responding to bad news

Is she? / Did you?

So what happened next?

Oh, I'm sorry to hear that.

Six years! / No way!

ERROR WARNING

Echo questions repeat the auxiliary, not the main verb:

She's moving back. → Is she? NOT Moves she? · They split up. → Did they? · I've met her. → Have you?
